nodes.label: Rhysida (RaaS)
nodes.notes: Ransomware-as-a-Service, active since 2023. Double-extortion. Ref: CISA AA23-319A, MITRE ATT&CK. Conceptual view — tactics only, no operational detail.

nodes.label: Phishing / valid accounts
nodes.notes: Initial access via phishing and legitimate compromised credentials (T1566, T1078).

nodes.label: External VPN — no MFA
nodes.notes: Exploitation of internet-facing services / VPNs lacking MFA (T1133, T1190).

nodes.label: Foothold Host
nodes.notes: Living-off-the-land: PowerShell, native tooling. Persistence via RDP & created accounts (T1021.001, T1136).

nodes.label: Domain Controller (ADDS)
nodes.notes: Privilege escalation — e.g. Zerologon (CVE-2020-1472) — to domain admin. Domain dominance enables backup destruction, vCenter login and GPO deployment (T1068, T1003).

nodes.label: AnyDesk (RMM)
nodes.notes: Legitimate remote-desktop / RMM software abused for resilient, low-detection persistent access — a fallback channel if the C2 beacon is caught (T1219 Remote Access Software).

nodes.label: File / App Servers
nodes.notes: Lateral movement with PsExec / RDP; log clearing & AV tampering to evade defence (T1021, T1070, T1562).

nodes.label: Attacker Exfil Store
nodes.notes: Sensitive data stolen BEFORE encryption — the leverage for double extortion (T1567 exfil over web service).

nodes.label: Veeam Backups — deleted
nodes.notes: Inhibit System Recovery (T1490): backup repositories located and destroyed so victims cannot restore — maximising extortion pressure.

nodes.label: vCenter / ESXi
nodes.notes: Attacker logs into vCenter with harvested AD credentials to reach the virtualization layer.

nodes.label: Virtual Machines
nodes.notes: VM datastores / ESXi encrypted directly (T1486) — takes out many servers at once.

nodes.label: Malicious GPO (ADDS)
nodes.notes: Domain Policy Modification (T1484.001): a rogue Group Policy Object pushes the encryptor to every domain-joined host at logon/startup — one-to-many deployment.

nodes.label: Rhysida Encryptor
nodes.notes: ChaCha20 + RSA-4096. Skips system dirs to keep hosts bootable (T1486 data encrypted for impact).

nodes.label: Encrypted File Shares
nodes.notes: Files renamed with .rhysida extension. Business operations halted.

nodes.label: CriticalBreachDetected.pdf
nodes.notes: PDF ransom note dropped on affected hosts (T1491).

nodes.label: Leak Site (double extortion)
nodes.notes: Victim named on a Tor leak/auction site; stolen data threatened for release to force payment.

steps.note: Rhysida — a ransomware-as-a-service crime group (active since 2023) known for double extortion. Conceptual kill chain mapped to MITRE ATT&CK / CISA AA23-319A.
1 · Initial Access. Rhysida gets in through phishing and valid stolen credentials, or by exploiting internet-facing services and VPNs that lack MFA.

2 · Foothold & Privilege Escalation. Establish a foothold with living-off-the-land tooling, then escalate — e.g. Zerologon — to take over the Domain Controller. Domain admin is the master key for everything that follows.

3 · C2, Discovery & Lateral Movement. A Cobalt Strike beacon calls home, and they also install AnyDesk — a legitimate RMM tool — for resilient, low-detection remote access. Operators use PsExec/RDP to spread across file and application servers, clearing logs and tampering with AV.
4 · Exfiltration. Sensitive data is STOLEN over the network before anything is encrypted — this is the leverage for the second extortion demand.
5a · Inhibit recovery. Using domain admin, they hunt down and DELETE the backups — typically the Veeam backup server — so the victim cannot simply restore (T1490).
5b · Hit the virtualization layer. They log into vCenter with harvested AD credentials and encrypt the VM datastores / ESXi directly — taking out many servers in one move (T1486).

5c · Mass deployment. Instead of running the encryptor host-by-host, they create a malicious Group Policy Object in Active Directory that pushes it to every domain-joined machine at logon (T1484.001).
5d · Encrypt & notify. The Rhysida encryptor (ChaCha20 + RSA-4096) encrypts file shares and drops the CriticalBreachDetected.pdf ransom note. Operations halt.
Double extortion. The victim is named on a Tor leak site and the stolen data is threatened for release — pressure to pay even with backups.

Full chain: access → domain admin → C2 & lateral → exfiltrate → destroy backups → encrypt VMs & shares (mass-deployed via GPO) → extort. Break it with: MFA everywhere, patching, tiered admin & GPO monitoring, immutable/offline backups, and egress control.
